# Final Assignment

## Overview

- An independent, take-home analysis
- One week to complete
- Uses the same study dataset
- Marked out of 100%

::: {.notes}
Introduce the capstone assessment.

Key teaching point: this consolidates all five days into one independent analysis.

Clinical interpretation: it mirrors writing the analysis for a real paper.

Audience question: how long should you budget? Expected: a few focused sessions across the week.

Demo tip: encourage starting from their saved Day 2 cleaning script.
:::

## Final Assignment - What to Do {.smaller}

### Task

| Working independently, analyse the study dataset and identify the determinants of treatment uptake.

### Your submission must

- Import the raw data and clean/validate it.
- Produce descriptive statistics and a publication-ready Table 1.
- Create at least two publication-quality figures.
- Perform appropriate statistical tests.
- Fit simple and multiple logistic regression models.
- Interpret the results and write a short Results section.
- Be fully reproducible (a single script that runs start to finish).

::: {.notes}
Spell out exactly what to deliver.

Key teaching point: reproducibility is graded - the script must run on a clean machine.

Common mistake: submitting only output with no script, or a script with hard-coded absolute paths.

Clinical interpretation: the Results section should read like a journal submission.

Audience question: what makes a script reproducible? Expected: relative paths, library() calls, set.seed, no manual steps.

Demo tip: point them to the Day 5 results draft as a template.
:::

## Final Assignment - Deliverables & Submission {.smaller}

### Submit

| 1. A single commented R script (.R) or R Markdown/Quarto file.
| 2. The exported Table 1 and figures.
| 3. A one-page Results section (about 250-400 words).

### Format

| Use an RStudio Project with relative paths.
| Name files clearly: Surname\_Phase1\_Assignment.R
| Email the .zip to the lead trainer, Vương Mỹ Lượng: myluong.1710\@gmail.com

::: {.callout-warning}
## Academic integrity
Work independently. You may use the course scripts and notes, but the analysis and writing must be your own.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clarify the mechanics of submission.

Key teaching point: clear, commented code is part of the grade, not an afterthought.

Common mistake: figures saved at screen resolution - require 300 dpi via ggsave.

Clinical interpretation: a tidy submission reflects a tidy analyst.

Audience question: R script or Quarto? Expected: either - Quarto earns the reproducibility marks easily.

Demo tip: show the folder structure you expect.
:::

## Marking Rubric (out of 100%) {.smaller}

| Component | What is assessed | Marks |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Data import & cleaning | Correct import, missing codes, validation, recoding | 20 |
| Descriptive statistics | Appropriate summaries and a correct Table 1 | 15 |
| Figures | Two clear, correctly labelled, publication-quality figures | 10 |
| Statistical tests | Right test chosen and correctly applied | 15 |
| Regression modelling | Sound univariable & multivariable logistic models | 20 |
| Interpretation & Results | Accurate ORs/CIs and clear clinical writing | 15 |
| Reproducibility & code quality | Runs end-to-end; clean, commented, relative paths | 5 |

: Total = 100%. A detailed marking guide is provided to instructors.

::: {.notes}
Make grading transparent.

Key teaching point: cleaning and regression carry the most weight (20 each) - spend time there.

Clinical interpretation: interpretation is explicitly rewarded, not just computation.

Common mistake: perfect code, wrong interpretation - you lose the 15 interpretation marks.

Audience question: where will you focus your effort? Expected: cleaning + modelling - correct.

Demo tip: the full marking guide with point-by-point criteria is in the instructor pack.
:::

## Marking Guide - What Earns Full Marks

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Strong submission

- Handles all messiness (dups, sentinels, impossible values).
- Table 1 stratified by uptake with sensible tests.
- Adjusted ORs with 95% CIs and correct reference levels.
- Results paragraph matches the numbers and is clinically framed.
- One script runs cleanly from raw data to outputs.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Common mark losses

- Leaving 999 / -99 as real numbers.
- Analysing all 1,500 instead of diagnosed patients.
- Reporting log-odds instead of odds ratios.
- Interpreting a non-significant result as 'no effect'.
- Absolute paths that break on another computer.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Give participants a concrete picture of excellent vs weak work.

Key teaching point: most marks are lost on avoidable cleaning and interpretation errors.

Clinical interpretation: 'not significant' means 'insufficient evidence', not 'no effect'.

Common mistake: forgetting to restrict to htn\_diagnosed == Yes for the uptake analysis.

Audience question: why analyse only diagnosed patients? Expected: uptake is only defined once diagnosed.

Demo tip: hand out this slide as a self-check before submission.
:::
